En álgebra, una expresión con $x$ era un: In algebra, an expression with $x$ was a machine: a number went in and another came out. In geometry, an equation in $x$ and $y$ was a picture. This block brings the two together under one name, function, and looks at them at once: the formula and its graph. Almost everything that follows — limits, derivatives, integrals — are questions about that graph.
Una <strong>función</strong> es una regl: A function is a rule assigning to each input value exactly one output value. It is a machine: you put a number in, another comes out, and always the same one for the same input.
Esa palabra, <em>único</em>, es toda la: That word, one, is the whole definition. If one input could correspond to two outputs, it would not be a function. Graphically that gives the quickest test there is:
<strong>Prueba de la recta vertical</str: The vertical line test: if any vertical line cuts the graph at more than one point, that is not a function. That is why a circle is not one.
Cómo reconocer una función de un vistazo: How to recognise a function at a glance
¿Define $y^2 = x$ una función $y$ de $x$: Does $y^2 = x$ define $y$ as a function of $x$?
Sí: es una ecuación con $x$ e $y$: Yes: it is an equation with $x$ and $y$
Tener ecuación no basta. Para $x = 4$ sa: Having an equation is not enough. For $x = 4$ two values come out, $y = 2$ and $y = -2$: two outputs for one input.
La recta vertical $x = 4$ corta la curva: The vertical line $x = 4$ cuts the curve at $(4, 2)$ and $(4, -2)$. $y = \sqrt{x}$ would be a function, keeping just one branch.
La idea de función tardó siglos en cuaja: The idea of a function took centuries to set. Leibniz used the word in 1673 to speak of segments attached to a curve; Euler wrote it as $f(x)$ in 1734 and understood it as a formula. Only in the nineteenth century, with Dirichlet, was the modern definition reached: a function need not be given by a formula, it is enough for the correspondence to be well defined. That leap opened the door to modern analysis.
Toda función tiene dos conjuntos asociad: Every function has two attached sets worth not confusing: where it can go in and where it can come out. The domain is the values of $x$ the function admits; the range, the values of $y$ it manages to reach. In practice the domain is worked out by looking for what is forbidden, which at this level is almost always one of these three things.
<strong>Dominio</strong> $\\operatorname: Domain $\operatorname{Dom} f$: the values of $x$ for which the function exists.
<strong>Recorrido</strong> (o imagen) $\: Range (or image) $\operatorname{Im} f$: all the values $f(x)$ manages to take.
Casi siempre el dominio son todos los re: Almost always the domain is all the reals minus the forbidden points. And there are only three prohibitions we know of so far:
Logaritmo de cero o negativo: Logarithm of zero or a negative

<strong>Localizar las prohibiciones.</st: Locate the prohibitions. There is a square root (what is inside cannot be negative) and a denominator (it cannot be zero). Two conditions, and both have to hold.

El dominio es la respuesta a «¿qué valor: The domain is the answer to “what values make sense here?”, and not considering it is a classic source of nonsense. A formula working out body mass index means nothing with a height of zero; a population growth model fitted with ten years of data is no use for predicting a hundred. Forms rejecting an impossible date of birth are checking a domain.
Lo que se lee en una gráfica: What you read in a graph
Una gráfica bien mirada cuenta casi todo: A graph, looked at properly, tells almost everything worth knowing about a function, and learning to interrogate it saves a great deal of calculation. These are the questions worth always asking it, in this order.
<strong>Cortes con los ejes</strong>: co: Crossings with the axes: with the y-axis, the value $f(0)$. With the x-axis, the solutions of $f(x)=0$ (the roots).
<strong>Crecimiento</strong>: la función: Increase: the function increases where the graph rises as you go right.
<strong>Máximos y mínimos</strong>: los: Maxima and minima: the peaks and the valleys.
<strong>Continuidad</strong>: si se pued: Continuity: whether it can be drawn without lifting the pencil.
<strong>Simetría</strong>: si es simétri: Symmetry: if it is symmetric about the y-axis it is called even ($f(-x)=f(x)$); if about the origin, odd ($f(-x)=-f(x)$).
Compara la curva con su reflejo. Si coin: Compare the curve with its reflection. If they agree on reflecting in the y-axis it is even; if they agree on turning a half turn about the origin it is odd.

Una función no tiene por qué comerse un: A function does not have to eat a number and give back another. It can eat the two coordinates of a point on the screen and give back a colour, and then its graph is the image. That is a shader, and the whole graphics programming block leans on that idea: [[gfx-pixel|the pixel that asks itself what colour it is]] starts right there, with a function of two variables written in three lines and a picture coming out of it.
Una función cuya gráfica es un cuadro: A function whose graph is a picture
Dos funciones se pueden <strong>encadena: Two functions can be chained: the output of one is used as the input of the other, like two machines in a row. It is the idea behind the [[fn-derivadas|chain rule]], and the one that lets complicated functions be built from simple ones.

The circle $\circ$ is read “composed with”: $g\circ f$ is “g composed with f” and is applied from right to left, first $f$ and then $g$. In general $g\circ f \ne f\circ g$: putting on socks and then shoes is not the same as the other way round.

$f^{-1}$ is read “f inverse” — not “f to the power minus one”, and it is not $\frac{1}{f}$ — and it is the function that undoes what $f$ does.
Con $f(x) = x + 1$ y $g(x) = x^2$, ¿cuán: With $f(x) = x + 1$ and $g(x) = x^2$, what is $(g\circ f)(2)$?
Eso es $f(g(2)) = 4 + 1$: primero el cua: That is $f(g(2)) = 4 + 1$: first the square and then adding. In $g\circ f$ it is $f$ that is applied first.
First $f(2) = 3$, then $g(3) = 9$. The function on the right acts first.
$3$ es solo $f(2)$. Falta aplicar $g$ al: $3$ is only $f(2)$. You still have to apply $g$ to the result.
Para calcular la inversa se escribe $y =: To work out the inverse you write $y = f(x)$, swap $x$ and $y$ and isolate the $y$. It exists only if $f$ does not repeat values (if it is [[lg-conjuntos|injective]]): if two inputs gave the same output, the inverse would not know which to go back to. And its graph is that of $f$ reflected in the line $y = x$, because swapping $x$ and $y$ is exactly that symmetry.

Saber leer una gráfica es una defensa ci: Knowing how to read a graph is a civic defence. Most misleading charts in circulation do not lie about the data: they lie about the axis. A vertical axis not starting at zero turns a 2 % rise into a cliff; a squeezed horizontal axis turns a gentle trend into an explosion. Looking at the axes first and the curve second is the habit that separates someone who understands a figure from someone who believes it.
